title: Overcoming the Modality Gap in Context-Aided Forecasting
claim: Contexts are produced and kept only if they verifiably improve forecasts, by sampling, generating, then filtering with a model.
layout: 3 colored panels, left-to-right, numbered stages with accept/reject branch
description: Three rounded, color-coded panels run left to right, numbered 1 to 3. Panel 1 (orange), 'Sampling a Window', shows a small time-series plot. A blue History line rises and an orange dashed Future line spikes and then falls. Points are labeled z1 through zP+Q. Under the plot is dataset metadata (Electricity Consumption, Daily) with a database icon. Panel 2 (blue), 'Generating Context', shows an LLM brain icon above a text box. The box holds a generated heatwave scenario describing a spike in electricity consumption. Panel 3 (green), 'Verifying Context', is a flow diagram. An LLM asks whether the context is valid and relevant. Two CAF Model branches, one given context plus history and one given history only, feed a 'Context helps?' decision. The decision ends in a green check (Accept) or a red X (Reject). The eye goes first to the colored headers and the example text.
caption: The data-augmentation pipeline: (1) From each source dataset, we sample forecasting windows consisting of a numerical history and prediction horizon, along with dataset metadata. (2) We generate scenario-style textual context conditioned on the window. (3) We verify context relevance by checking whether a strong CAF method achieves better predictions with context than without (e.g., lower CRPS); windows are accepted if context improves predictions and rejected otherwise.
abstract: Context-aided forecasting (CAF) holds promise for integrating domain knowledge and forward-looking information, enabling AI systems to surpass traditional statistical methods. However, recent empirical studies reveal a puzzling gap: multimodal models often fail to outperform their unimodal counterparts. We hypothesize that this underperformance stems from poor context quality in existing datasets, as verification is challenging. To address these limitations, we introduce a semi-synthetic data augmentation method that generates contexts both descriptive of temporal dynamics and verifiably complementary to numerical histories. This approach enables massive-scale dataset creation, resulting in CAF-7M, a corpus of 7 million context-augmented time series windows, including a rigorously verified test set. We demonstrate that semi-synthetic pre-training transfers effectively to real-world evaluation, and show clear evidence of context utilization. Our results suggest that dataset quality, rather than architectural limitations, has been the primary bottleneck in context-aided forecasting.
